questions.q: An order controller does all of the jobs below in one request. Which are safe to move to a queue?
questions.hint: For each one, ask: if this happened ten seconds later, would the customer lose anything?

options.text: Sending the order confirmation email
options.why: An email arriving a few seconds late hurts nobody, and if it fails you can retry.

options.text: Saving the order row to the database
options.why: Without it you have no order number to give the customer. The response needs this step.

options.text: Generating the invoice PDF
options.why: It is heavy work, and the customer isn't asking for the PDF this second. A worker can build it in the background.

options.text: Checking and reserving stock
options.why: The customer needs the "out of stock" answer right now. Delaying it means first telling them a false "order successful".

options.text: Booking the courier through their API
options.why: An external API is slow and fragile. In a queue, orders can still be taken while it is down, and the booking is retried later.

questions.q: Which of these names is an event rather than a command?
questions.hint: Which name describes something that has already happened?

options.text: SendInvoiceEmail
options.why: It is an order: "send the email". The job hasn't happened yet, so it is a command.

options.text: PaymentFailed
options.why: A fact stated in the past tense. What happens next, whether telling the customer or canceling the order, is not decided by the sender.

options.text: GenerateSalesReport
options.why: It starts with a verb and is an order; exactly one handler will do it. That makes it a command.

options.text: BookCourier
options.why: "Book a courier" is an order for one specific job, so it is a command.

questions.q: The ChargeOrder message is routed to an async transport. What is wrong with this controller?
questions.hint: When the response goes out, has the worker started the job yet?

options.text: It says "paid" before any money is taken; it should return 202 and "pending"
options.why: dispatch() only writes the message to the queue. The job runs later and may fail, so the honest answer is pending.

options.text: flush() is never called after dispatch(), so the message won't be sent
options.why: dispatch() writes the message to the transport by itself; it doesn't need the EntityManager's flush().

options.text: The message should carry the whole $order entity instead of the id
options.why: The opposite: passing the id is correct. An entity would reach the worker as a stale copy.

options.text: Payments can never be handled through a queue
options.why: They can, and many systems do. The one condition is that you tell the user the true state (pending).

questions.q: In a marketplace, three teams (analytics, fraud, search) each read every order event at their own pace. A new team will want to read the last 7 days of events from the beginning. What fits?
questions.hint: Which setup keeps messages after they are read, and gives each reader its own bookmark?

options.text: One RabbitMQ queue that workers from all three teams consume together
options.why: In one queue, each message goes to just one of the workers. Once one team gets it, the other two never see it.

options.text: A Kafka-style stream, with each team as its own consumer group
options.why: A stream keeps messages until retention runs out. Each group reads from its own offset, and a new group can replay from the start.

options.text: Direct HTTP calls from the controller to each team's service
options.why: The order request would then depend on the speed and health of three services, and replaying old events would be impossible.

options.text: A cron job every minute that scans the orders table and notifies everyone
options.why: Scanning is slow, events get missed or sent twice, and you would have to track by hand how far each team has read, which a stream does for you.

questions.q: Rima wrote the handler and a worker is running. Yet the request is as slow as ever, and messenger:stats always shows an empty queue. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Does the message ever reach the transport?

options.text: The worker isn't fast enough
options.why: A slow worker would let messages pile up in the queue. An empty queue means messages never get there.

options.text: The message class isn't listed in routing, so the handler runs inside the request
options.why: Without routing, Messenger sends the message to no transport and runs the handler inside dispatch().

options.text: The handler is missing #[AsMessageHandler]
options.why: Then Messenger would find no handler and throw an exception. The work wouldn't silently happen inside the request.

options.text: The Doctrine transport doesn't support async work
options.why: It does. The Doctrine transport uses a database table as the queue, and it is enough for a small app.

questions.q: Which of these are true costs of making work async?
questions.hint: Think about how much control you keep over a job once it is in the queue.

options.text: You can't say in advance exactly when the job will finish
options.why: A backlog or busy workers add delay, so the user sees the old state for a while.

options.text: The same message may arrive twice, and the handler has to be ready for that
options.why: If a worker dies midway, the queue redelivers the message. So the handler must be harmless when run twice.

options.text: Async work no longer needs a database transaction
options.why: The writes inside the handler still have to succeed or fail together. Async is no replacement for that.

options.text: When it fails, the user is no longer on the page, so you need another way to tell them
options.why: In a request you can show an error on screen. A failed async job needs a notification, a status page or a retry.

questions.q: New code has been deployed, but the background jobs still behave the old way. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: A web request loads the code fresh each time. Does a worker?

options.text: The messages waiting in the queue carried the old code with them
options.why: A message holds only data, not code. The worker process decides which code runs.

options.text: The worker is a long-running process and keeps the old code in memory until restarted
options.why: A worker reads the code once and runs for hours. Running messenger:stop-workers after a deploy makes it restart with the new code.

options.text: The transport DSN needs to change
options.why: The DSN decides where messages are stored. It has nothing to do with which version of the code runs.

questions.q: A handler sends an email and dies before the ack. What happens next?
questions.hint: Think about what the broker knows and what it doesn't.

options.text: The message is lost and the email is never sent again
options.why: That is at-most-once behavior. When the ack comes after the work, the message isn't lost.

options.text: The broker delivers the message again, and the customer may get two emails
options.why: No ack arrived, so the broker assumes the job wasn't done. It actually was done, so you get a duplicate.

options.text: The broker figures out the email went out and won't send it again
options.why: The broker can't see inside the handler. It only knows whether an ack arrived.

questions.q: Which statements are correct?
questions.hint: Is the ack before or after the work, and what is the handler's responsibility?

options.text: In at-least-once, the ack is sent after the work
options.why: With the ack after the work, a crash makes the message come again, so it is never lost.

options.text: In at-most-once, a message can be lost
options.why: With the ack first, after a crash the broker thinks the job is done when it isn't.

options.text: Exactly-once means the handler no longer needs to be idempotent
options.why: A broker can't guarantee that outside work, like an email or payment, runs only once.

options.text: At-least-once never loses a message and never delivers one twice
options.why: The chance of a duplicate is exactly its price, and it is what forces the handler to be idempotent.

questions.q: In a banking app you want each account's transactions processed in order, but all accounts at the same time. What do you do?
questions.hint: You need order only within one account.

options.text: Run just one worker for all messages
options.why: The order holds, but every account gets stuck in one line.

options.text: Use accountId as the partition key or message group id
options.why: One account runs in order on one line, and different accounts run in parallel.

options.text: Put a timestamp in each message and let the worker sort them out
options.why: Clocks on different machines don't agree, and you have no way to handle a later message arriving first.

questions.q: What is wrong with the handler below?
questions.hint: What happens to the balance if the message arrives twice?

options.text: On a redelivery the same money is credited twice
options.why: There is no duplicate check, so under at-least-once the second message adds the amount again.

options.text: Because it is `final readonly`, the handler won't work
options.why: That is fine. `readonly` works on Messenger handlers.

options.text: Two workers can read the same balance and overwrite each other's credit
options.why: Both read 100 and write 100 plus their own amount, so one credit is lost. A single `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + :amount` avoids that.

options.text: Reading the entity with `find()` is wrong
options.why: Reading a fresh entity by id is the right approach.

questions.q: What happens if you give every message the same `MessageGroupId` on SQS FIFO?
questions.hint: Messages in one group run one after another.

options.text: Order is guaranteed, but throughput drops to about that of a single worker
options.why: Every message runs in order inside one group, with no parallelism.

options.text: Messages run faster, because SQS spreads them out by group id
options.why: A group id doesn't spread messages out. It ties one group to one line.

options.text: Duplicate messages stop completely
options.why: The deduplication id prevents duplicates, not the group id, and only for a limited time.

questions.q: A handler skips any message whose version is not newer than the stored one. Which messages can it safely skip?
questions.hint: Skip a message only if a newer one already says everything it says.

options.text: AddressChanged: the customer's complete new address, version 7
options.why: It carries the whole state, so a newer address message replaces it entirely.

options.text: StockDecreased: 3 units sold, version 12
options.why: It carries only a change. Skipping it because it is late leaves stock 3 too high.

options.text: BalanceSnapshot: the account balance is now 180, version 4
options.why: A snapshot of the full balance. If version 5 already arrived, version 4 holds nothing new.

options.text: PointsEarned: +20 loyalty points, version 9
options.why: Another change message. Dropping it silently removes 20 points. Store its id instead.

questions.q: In which cases is a retry pointless, so the message should go straight to the failure transport?
questions.hint: In which cases will time passing change nothing?

options.text: The SMS gateway times out for 30 seconds
options.why: That is a temporary failure. Once the gateway recovers, a retry will succeed.

options.text: The phone number in the message has an invalid format
options.why: The number won't fix itself, so retrying is pointless.

options.text: The database hits a deadlock for a few seconds
options.why: A deadlock is temporary. A retry usually clears it quietly.

options.text: The data in the message JSON has the wrong type and no handler can read it
options.why: The data is broken, so it will fail every time you run it. That is a permanent failure too.

questions.q: In the config below, what happens to a failed message once `max_retries` is used up?
questions.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        transports:
            async:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                retry_strategy:
                    max_retries: 3
                    delay: 1000
                    multiplier: 2
questions.hint: Is there a failure_transport line?

options.text: It automatically creates a failed queue and collects there
options.why: You have to define the failure transport yourself; Messenger doesn't create one on its own.

options.text: The message is discarded and nobody even sees it
options.why: With no `failure_transport` set, the message is thrown away after the retries. The work is lost silently.

options.text: It keeps retrying forever, at gaps of 1s, 2s, 4s
options.why: `max_retries: 3` sets the limit. After that there are no more retries.

questions.q: A handler adds loyalty points every time it runs. What happens on a redelivery, and what should you do?
questions.hint: How will the handler recognize a message it has seen before?

options.text: Points are added twice; keep the message id in a processed_message table with a UNIQUE constraint and check it
options.why: An idempotent consumer: if the id has been seen, the handler does nothing.

options.text: Messenger spots duplicates itself and drops them, so there is nothing to do
options.why: Messenger doesn't know what the work means. Handling duplicates is the handler's responsibility.

options.text: Turning off retries means there will be no more duplicates
options.why: Even with retries off, a crash still causes a redelivery, and you take on the risk of losing work.

questions.q: Which statements are correct?
questions.hint: Think about what backoff and the DLQ are for.

options.text: Backoff gives a failing service time to recover
options.why: An immediate retry presses harder on a failing service. A growing gap lets it breathe.

options.text: You should raise an alert when messages land in the DLQ
options.why: A DLQ means work for a human. With no alert, the work quietly rots there.

options.text: The more retries the better, so keep `max_retries` large
options.why: A big number sends a broken message round for hours. Keep the limit small and move it to the DLQ.

options.text: Messages in the DLQ fix themselves and run again
options.why: Someone has to fix the cause and then run `messenger:failed:retry`.

questions.q: Why keep the UNIQUE constraint on (message_id, handler) and the work in one transaction?
questions.hint: What if the work is done but the ledger entry isn't written, or the reverse?

options.text: So the ledger entry and the work either both happen or both are canceled
options.why: Kept apart, a crash could leave the mark made but the work not done, or the work done but no mark.

options.text: So the database runs faster
options.why: This is for correctness, not speed.

options.text: So Messenger never lets a duplicate message into the queue
options.why: The message gets into the queue anyway. The duplicate is caught inside the handler, not on the way in.

questions.q: A payment gateway is down for about 10 minutes. Messenger is on its defaults: 3 retries at 1s, 2s and 4s. What happens to the messages?
questions.hint: Add up how long the retries last.

options.text: They use up their retries in about 7 seconds and land in the failure transport
options.why: 1 + 2 + 4 is 7 seconds, far short of 10 minutes. Raise `delay` and `max_retries` to cover the outage.

options.text: They wait quietly until the gateway is back, then succeed
options.why: Retries stop after `max_retries`. Nothing waits for the gateway.

options.text: Messenger notices the outage and pauses all retries
options.why: Messenger does not know why a handler failed. Each message follows its own retry schedule.

questions.q: The app runs on two servers, each with a Scheduler worker. The 2 a.m. report is released twice every night. What is the fix?
questions.hint: If two workers try to release a message at the same moment, who wins?

options.text: Add a lock to the schedule so only one worker releases the message at a time
options.why: The Scheduler's `lock()` exists for exactly this.

options.text: Keep one server's worker switched off and never start it
options.why: If that server dies, all the work stops. It is no real fix.

options.text: Change the time from 2:00 to 2:01
options.why: Changing the time doesn't help; both servers will still release the message together at the new time.

questions.q: A job takes up to 5 minutes. The SQS visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
questions.hint: What is the message's state after 30 seconds?

options.text: The job stops by itself after 30 seconds
options.why: The timeout doesn't stop the worker; it only makes the message visible again.

options.text: The first worker keeps going while another worker takes the message and starts the same job
options.why: After 30 seconds the message becomes visible again, and a second worker picks up the same job.

options.text: The message is lost forever
options.why: It isn't lost. It becomes visible again, and that is what causes the duplicate.

questions.q: What problems does this handler have?
questions.hint: Think about memory, time, and what happens on a crash.

options.text: All entities load into memory, and with hundreds of thousands it runs out
options.why: `findAll()` fetches every row at once.

options.text: A crash midway leaves no checkpoint, so everything restarts from the beginning
options.why: Progress is written nowhere, so every retry starts from the first row.

options.text: Calling `markDone` at the end is wrong; it should be called at the start
options.why: Saying "done" when the work finishes is right. Saying it at the start would show a false state.

options.text: The handler can't use `$m->jobId`
options.why: A message's plain fields can be used in the handler.

questions.q: OTP messages and the monthly report share one queue. While the report runs, OTPs arrive late. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Which work is hurt by delay, and which isn't?

options.text: A separate high transport for OTPs and low for reports, with workers reading high first
options.why: Urgent messages no longer get stuck behind slow work.

options.text: Switch the report off
options.why: The work is needed; you only have to move it to its own lane.

options.text: Run 10 times as many workers, with no separate queue
options.why: It costs more, and the same problem returns when the reports grow. A separate lane is the real fix.

questions.q: Only 5 messages are waiting in the queue, yet you suspect a worker is stuck. Which measure shows it?
questions.hint: Even when the number is small, something may have been sitting there for a long time.

options.text: Queue depth, the number of messages
options.why: A small number can look healthy while one message has been stuck for hours.

options.text: The age of the oldest message
options.why: A stuck message keeps getting older. It exposes the delay even when the count is low.

options.text: The worker's CPU usage alone
options.why: A stuck worker may be waiting on I/O, with low CPU, so this tells you nothing.

questions.q: Two servers run Scheduler workers with `->lock(...)`, yet the report is still released twice. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Where does each server keep its lock?

options.text: The lock store is local to each server, so neither sees the other's lock
options.why: A lock only excludes workers that look at the same store. Point `framework.lock` at Redis or the database.

options.text: The cron expression is wrong
options.why: The time is right. The same slot is released twice because two workers both think they hold the lock.

options.text: Messenger retries the message
options.why: A retry only happens after a failure, and here both releases succeed.

questions.q: Your app has workers on 3 servers and `cache.app` is the default filesystem cache. The deploy runs `messenger:stop-workers` on server 1 only. Which changes make all servers pick up the new code?
questions.hint: The signal travels through the cache, and each server has its own disk.

options.text: Point `cache.app` at a Redis that all servers use
options.why: Then the mark written by the one command is visible to every worker.

options.text: Run the stop command on every server during the deploy
options.why: Each server writes the mark into its own cache, and its own workers read it. The price is that the script must not skip a server.

options.text: Run `cache:clear` on server 1 after the deploy
options.why: That clears server 1's cache only. It does not tell workers on other servers anything.

options.text: Raise `numprocs` on servers 2 and 3
options.why: More processes of the old code are still old code.

questions.q: You need 60 jobs a second and each job takes 0.25 s. How many workers must be busy at all times?
questions.hint: Multiply jobs per second by the seconds each job takes.

options.text: 4 workers, because each does 4 jobs a second
options.why: That is the speed of one worker. You still need 60 ÷ 4 workers to match the arrivals.

options.text: 60 workers, one for every job per second
options.why: That ignores that a worker finishes a job in 0.25 s and takes the next. It wastes memory and connections.

options.text: About 15, plus some headroom for spikes
options.why: 60 × 0.25 = 15 workers busy. Headroom of about 30% brings it to around 20.

questions.q: Workers run for days and memory keeps growing until the server kills them. What is missing from this config?
questions.code:
[program:messenger-async]
command=php bin/console messenger:consume async
numprocs=9
autorestart=true
questions.hint: autorestart only helps after a process exits. What makes it exit before the crash?

options.text: `--memory-limit`, so a worker exits cleanly once it passes a cap
options.why: It checks memory between messages and exits, and the supervisor starts a fresh one.

options.text: `--time-limit`, so no worker lives longer than a set time
options.why: It bounds the lifetime of any leak, and it also limits how long old code can run.

options.text: Nothing, `autorestart=true` already restarts leaky workers
options.why: It restarts a process only after it exits. A worker that keeps growing never exits by itself.

options.text: Set `numprocs=1`
options.why: Each worker still leaks. You only lose capacity.

questions.q: Why does this fail on 3 servers, but not on 1?
questions.hint: Where does the next worker run, and where is the file?

options.text: The next worker may run on another server, where that path does not exist
options.why: The file is on one machine's disk. The queue gives the next job to any worker.

options.text: Messenger loses messages when a path is sent
options.why: The message arrives fine. It points to a file that is not there.

options.text: PHP cannot write files from a worker
options.why: Workers can write files. The problem is where the file ends up.

questions.q: After you add 5 more servers, the main database slows down although the queue is empty most of the time. You use the Doctrine transport. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: What does an idle worker do every second?

options.text: Every worker polls the messages table in your main database, and each one holds a connection
options.why: Load from polling and connections grows with the number of workers, even when there is little work.

options.text: The Doctrine transport stops working above 10 workers
options.why: There is no such limit. The cost is load on the shared database.

options.text: The stop signal makes workers restart in a loop
options.why: That only happens when the signal fires, which is once per deploy.

questions.q: Ryan starts `messenger:consume async` on 3 servers. Must he change code so that each message is handled by just one worker?
questions.hint: Think about what the shared transport does with a message.

options.text: Yes, give each server its own queue
options.why: Separate queues would split the work by hand. A shared queue already shares it.

options.text: No, each message goes to one worker. But a crash can cause redelivery, so handlers should be idempotent
options.why: The transport hands a message to one worker at a time, and delivery is at-least-once, so a duplicate is still possible.

options.text: Yes, every message reaches all three, so he must add a lock
options.why: Competing consumers do not receive copies. They take turns.

options.text: No, and duplicates are now impossible
options.why: Duplicates can still happen after a crash or a visibility timeout.

questions.q: The plan: 6 servers with 9 workers each, a web app that peaks at 40 connections, PostgreSQL at its default limit. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: Workers times servers, plus the web app, against 100.

options.text: Raise `--memory-limit` on every worker
options.why: Memory is not the issue here, connections are.

options.text: 54 worker connections plus 40 for the web is 94, which is close; one more server breaks it. Run fewer workers or add a pooler
options.why: 6 × 9 = 54, plus 40 gives 94 of 100. Count the budget first, then cut workers or add a pooler such as PgBouncer.

options.text: Workers share one connection, so there is no problem
options.why: Each worker process holds about one connection of its own.

questions.q: One order sends five SMS and the user is annoyed. Which fixes are right?
questions.hint: Does every event need to be its own message the moment it happens?

options.text: Collect the small events in a digest and send one summary
options.why: When several small updates go in one message, the count drops and no information is lost.

options.text: Check the user's preferences and send only on the channel they want
options.why: Respecting preferences removes the messages on unwanted channels.

options.text: Turn SMS off and keep only email, for everyone
options.why: That hurts both urgent messages and users who prefer SMS.

options.text: Wait 5 seconds before each event
options.why: Waiting doesn't reduce the number of messages, it only delays them.

questions.q: Which is the correct order for the pipeline?
questions.hint: Decide first, send afterwards.

options.text: Check preferences, then dedup/throttle, then send to the provider
options.why: Unwanted or duplicate messages are dropped before they reach the provider, which also saves cost.

options.text: Send to the provider, then check preferences
options.why: Checking preferences after sending is pointless; the message has already gone.

options.text: Dedup, then send, then preferences last
options.why: Send without respecting preferences and users who opted out still get the message.

questions.q: SMS provider A is often down. How do you stop OTPs being lost?
questions.hint: How can you name two providers in the DSN?

options.text: Change the DSN to `failover(%env(SMS_PROVIDER_A_DSN)% %env(SMS_PROVIDER_B_DSN)%)`
options.why: When A fails, Notifier tries B itself, with no code changes.

options.text: Swallow the failure in a try/catch when sending the OTP
options.why: Swallow the failure and the OTP never goes out, and nobody knows.

options.text: Send through both providers every time
options.why: The user gets two OTPs and the cost doubles. Failover is for when the first one fails.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?
questions.hint: What happens if sending fails after the mark is set?

options.text: If sending fails the mark stays, so the retry skips it and the message is never sent
options.why: The mark was set but nothing was sent. The retry will see "already sent" and return.

options.text: `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` can't prevent duplicates
options.why: The UNIQUE constraint together with this clause does prevent duplicates.

options.text: Returning is wrong; it should throw an exception
options.why: Quietly dropping the duplicate is right; it isn't a failure.

questions.q: Which messages may still go out (on an urgent channel) after the user has opted out of SMS?
questions.hint: Without the message, the user can't do what they came to do.

options.text: A password-reset OTP
options.why: It is transactional; without it the user can't get into their account.

options.text: A promotion for a new offer
options.why: Marketing must always honor opt-out.

options.text: A security alert about a suspicious login
options.why: It matters for account safety, so it is usually kept outside opt-out.

options.text: The weekly newsletter
options.why: It is promotional, and the user can switch it off if they want.

questions.q: Rachel switched off every notification. She asks for a password-reset code, and the pipeline obeys preferences for every kind of message. What happens?
questions.hint: What does `enabledChannels()` return when everything is off?

options.text: The pipeline sends the code anyway, because OTP is special
options.why: Nothing in this code treats an OTP differently. Without an explicit rule, it is just another message.

options.text: The code is sent to her email instead
options.why: She switched email off too, so the list of channels is empty and nothing is sent.

options.text: No code is sent, no error shows, and she is locked out
options.why: An empty channel list ends the pipeline quietly. A transactional kind must bypass preferences.

options.text: The code is queued and sent when she switches notifications back on
options.why: Nothing queues it. The message is dropped, and an expired OTP would be useless later anyway.

questions.q: In the digest job, `clear()` runs before `send()`. The email provider fails during that run. What is the result?
questions.hint: Which comes first: removing the items or delivering them?

options.text: The items are gone and the user never hears about them
options.why: The send failed after the items were removed, so nothing is left to retry. Clear only after a successful send.

options.text: The items stay and go out in the next run
options.why: That is what happens when `clear()` comes after `send()`. Here they were removed first.

options.text: The user gets the digest twice
options.why: Duplicates come from a crash after sending. Here nothing was sent at all.
